planting.note: Direct-sow in fall into a deep scree or alpine trough with grit to 12+ inches; protect from winter wet and summer humidity with an overhang rather than mulch.

directions: A Sierra Nevada endemic restricted to decomposed granite fellfields above treeline on Mount Whitney and the High Sierra crest, this plant carries striking silvery, cylindrical 'mousetail' foliage and bright yellow flowers. Success depends almost entirely on replicating sharp mineral drainage and cool root zones, so a deep scree bed or alpine trough with substantial grit is essential. Expect very slow establishment and treat any seed-grown plant as experimental, since documented nursery success is limited and this is a true specialist rather than a mainstream garden plant.

planting.note: Direct-sow with 3-4 weeks cold stratification into a vertical crevice or under a rock overhang so rain runs off the foliage rather than sitting on it.

directions: A classic small mat-forming alpine mustard explicitly called a desirable rock garden subject by experienced growers, this species carries masses of small yellow flowers in summer over a tight foliage mat. Rock-garden experience with the genus shows Draba species are slow and temperamental, with rosette rot from winter wet as the main failure mode rather than cold. Use a scree mix heavy in grit with minimal organic matter and avoid disturbing it once established.

planting.note: Direct-sow or divide the rhizomatous clump in spring into gritty, lean soil in full sun; avoid rich garden soil, which causes lax, rot-prone growth.

directions: Striking silvery, silky-haired rosette foliage stays attractive even out of bloom, with solitary yellow disc-flower heads on short stalks giving a tidy, distinctive alpine-meadow look. Unlike many true cushion-forming fellfield alpines, this species is a rhizomatous clump-former that can be lifted and divided to multiply stock once established. It tolerates more summer dryness than most high-alpine companions, making it a comparatively forgiving entry point into Sierra alpine cultivation.

planting.note: Root non-flowering cushion shoots as cuttings and plant into a slightly calcareous scree mix under an overhang or glass cover in wet-winter climates; winter wet, not cold, is the main killer.

directions: A true cushion-forming alpine phlox prized by rock gardeners, this species bears fragrant lavender-to-white flowers directly on the cushion surface. It favors limestone and travertine outcrops in the wild, so unlike most Sierra fellfield plants it benefits from a slightly calcareous scree mix with dolomitic lime chips rather than pure granite grit. Propagate named garden stock vegetatively from non-flowering cushion shoots rather than relying on seed, which is notoriously slow and erratic in this genus.

planting.note: Direct-sow into sharp scree conditions matching other high-alpine Polemonium; source seed only from ethical, ex-situ conservation stock given this species' rarity.

directions: A rare, fragrant alpine relative of skunkweed with a striking disjunct range across the White, Inyo, and Sweetwater Mountains plus a remote Klamath population, this species is a genuine botanical curiosity restricted to exposed talus and fellfield. It is essentially untested in the nursery trade — not described anywhere as biologically impossible to grow, simply undocumented in cultivation — so treat any attempt as experimental using the same sharp scree conditions as other high-alpine Polemonium. Given its CNPS rare-plant ranking, pursue only ethically sourced seed rather than wild collection.
sources: US Fish and Wildlife Service species profile

planting.note: Cold stratify seed in the refrigerator 3-4 weeks, then sow barely covered since light is required for germination; plant into a scree bed with a constant subsurface moisture source.

directions: A beloved rock-garden classic, this woody-based subshrub primrose roots directly into granite crevices fed by snowmelt seepage, producing showy pink flowers each spring. The key to success is that well-drained does not mean dry — the scree bed needs a constant subsurface moisture source even though the surface grit stays dry-looking. Give it morning sun and afternoon shade to avoid the combination of high light and surface heat that stresses the shallow root crown, and divide established offsets for a faster path to flowering than seed.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or divide offsets in spring into loose, gritty, well-drained rock-garden or container soil; water infrequently but deeply rather than frequent shallow watering.

directions: The most garden-ready plant of the Sierra alpine specialists, this true succulent rosette sedum carries attractive blue-green-to-red foliage and white to yellow-green flowers, well suited to standard rock gardens and containers rather than scree-level drainage perfection. It roots readily from stem cuttings or division, the method actual nurseries use, and establishes and spreads within one growing season. It needs no supplemental fertilization and tolerates ordinary rock-garden conditions far better than most of its true fellfield neighbors.

planting.note: Direct-sow with 60-90 days cold stratification into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; source seed or divisions from a low, mat-forming fellfield population for a true alpine-habit plant.

directions: Occurring as both an upright subalpine-meadow form and a low, spreading mat form at true alpine fellfield and talus elevations to nearly 13,000 feet, this species carries dark purple-blue tubular flowers in glandular clusters. Give it full sun and lean, fast-draining soil; established plants tolerate real summer drought once rooted, reflecting their native talus habitat. Avoid winter mulch that traps moisture around the crown, since this is a cold-hardy but wet-intolerant species.
